prize_parts.citation: for the development of orthogonal translation systems that expand the genetic code and allow site-specific incorporation of noncanonical amino acids into proteins in living cells

statement.case_for: Genetic code expansion is a general chemical handle on protein structure and function. The orthogonal tRNA/synthetase concept was first made to work in vivo by Schultz and Wang, and Chin extended it to multiple codons, orthogonal ribosomes and whole animals. It has been independently reproduced for over two decades, and it is now routine for installing spectroscopic probes, photocrosslinkers and catalytic groups in enzymes. Its interpretation is stable and it has no clinical-validation question hanging over it. The roles divide cleanly: founding concept and first demonstration (Schultz, Wang), then generalisation to multicellular systems and recoded genomes (Chin). That gives a coherent three-person configuration that stays inside the cap. Eight of eight members placed it in their top seven, and five placed it in their top three, which suggests it is the broadest common ground on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field never had one decisive breakthrough moment, and the credit is diffuse. Mehl and Yokoyama made real contributions and are left out by a three-name cap. Mehl's role in the early eukaryotic and E. coli systems, and Yokoyama's structural and engineering work on synthetases, are not trivial. There is also no single therapeutic application that would make the prize obviously consequential, and the field is close to the biomolecular-tool prizes of 2018, 2020 and 2024. If the committee wants the most conceptually novel and transformative mode of action on the list, targeted protein degradation is a serious rival, and my own ranking of it second reflects that.

responses.point: Daniel Aili ranks targeted protein degradation first, with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, because the idea is original and has opened an undruggable-target therapeutic field, and he treats the PROTAC and molecular-glue arms as one prize.
responses.response: I agree on the originality and on the importance of the thalidomide-cereblon mechanism, but I see a real attribution problem he treats too lightly. Handa's cereblon work belongs to the glue lineage. Ciulli's VHL ligands and ternary-complex structural work are what made rational PROTAC design possible. Choosing Handa over Ciulli, or the reverse, is a decision about the scope of the discovery and not a bookkeeping matter. With no approved degrader, I also think the prize would be awarded before the clinical case is closed. I would rather see the committee wait than settle credit now between two arms that are still developing.

responses.point: Peter Somfai puts Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first, with Buchwald and Hartwig, citing three decades of confirmation, enormous practical reach and a clean two-person attribution, and notes that the 2010 prize did not cover C-N coupling.
responses.response: The maturity and the clean two-person credit are real strengths, and I accept that the work is of very high quality. My reservation is not scientific merit but novelty within the prize record. Having honoured Pd cross-coupling in 2010, the committee would be rewarding a close successor to a prize it has already given, with Kosugi's earlier precedent adding a priority complication. Genetic code expansion is a different capability: it changes what proteins can contain, not how a bond is made. For that reason I keep B068 outside my preferred configuration, though I would not call it a weak candidate.

responses.point: Johan Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello dynamics first, as a clean two-person, long-validated foundation of ab initio simulation that is arguably overdue, and ranks genetic code expansion third as a timely biomolecular tool.
responses.response: I share his view that Car and Parrinello have an unambiguous origin and four decades of validation, and the attribution is neater than for my own choice. Where we differ is on how widely the discovery is felt. B037 has been supported by only one member, so it is unlikely to build a majority, and I think the committee should be honest about that. I am glad he agrees that B054 is timely, and I would add that the mechanistic probes it enables, such as site-specific spectroscopic labels in cytochrome-type enzymes, are a concrete case of the method answering physical-chemical questions.

responses.point: Andrei Chabes ranks degradation first, then phosphoramidite oligonucleotide synthesis, then base editing, and says base editors face maturity questions about long-term safety and off-target effects, and might be better recognised together with prime editing.
responses.response: I agree that base editing is still maturing on safety and off-target data, and that it sits uncomfortably close to the 2020 CRISPR prize. That is why I place it behind B054 even though I support the three-person Liu, Komor, Gaudelli configuration. I disagree somewhat about the case for waiting for prime editing. That would widen the scope and make the credit harder, and a prize that bundles base and prime editing would make the lead-author roles harder to separate. Genetic code expansion has the advantage that it has already had twenty years to settle.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a three-name cap that excludes Mehl and Yokoyama, whose contributions to early systems and synthetase engineering are real.

Whether protein-degradation credit can be split defensibly between PROTAC and molecular-glue lineages by the time this prize is decided, and whether the absence of an approved degrader is disqualifying.
Whether the 2018, 2020 and 2024 biomolecular-tool prizes make a further chemical-biology tool prize look repetitive.
Whether the wording of a citation for B054 can be written in a way that is distinct from the 2018 directed-evolution prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Xiaodong Zou, but she is a committee member and not a candidate, so no recusal issue arises. My own research on respiratory enzymes would use genetic-code-expansion tools, but I have no documented collaboration with any credited name.
